newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court asks Justice Dept. race case views.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court asks Justice Dept. race case views.

text.p: The Supreme Court asked the Justice Department on Tuesday for its views on whether a school district may cite racial diversity in laying off a white teacher over an equally qualified black teacher.

At issue is an appeal by the board of education in Piscataway, New Jersey arguing that employers may consider race as a factor in layoff decisions, for purposes other than to remedy past discrimination.

The school board argued that fostering diversity on a high school faculty was a lawful purpose and said consideration of race in layoff decisions does not invariably violate the rights of white employees.
The case gained prominence in 1994 when the Justice Department changed its position and supported affirmative action programmes designed to increase racial diversity.

Under the Bush administration, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division had backed the discrimination lawsuit by Sharon Taxman, the white business teacher at the high school who lost her job in 1989.
The Clinton Justice Department switched its support to the school board. But a U.S. appeals court rejected the department's filing, and it dropped out of the case.
Although the Justice Department initially did not take a position before the Supreme Court, Attorney General Janet Reno last week said the earlier filing "speaks for itself."
But the Supreme Court specifically requested that the Justice Department "file a brief in this case expressing the views of the United States."
The department's position could take several months, meaning the high court will not be able to hear arguments and decide the case during its current term which ends in June.
The Supreme Court in recent years has moved to restrict government affirmative action programmes, which flourished in the 1960s and 1970s as a way to remedy past discrimination.

The high court in June 1995 restricted federal affirmative action programmes for racial minorities, setting tough new standards before the government can pursue preferences for blacks or other minorities.
The Piscataway school board asked the Supreme Court to hear the case after a U.S. appeals court ruled the affirmative action policy violated the rights of white employees.
"The court should reject a blanket prohibition on consideration of race in layoffs," school board attorney David Rubin said in the appeal.

He said the case "has become the lightning rod in a stormy national debtate over whether" the federal civil rights law allows schools to consider race in employment decisions "to foster a diverse learning environment."

The school laid off Taxman instead of black teacher Debra Williams, who had been hired on the same day in 1980. Williams was the only black teacher in the business education department. Taxman returned to work in 1991 when another position opened up in the business department.
